name: Tuareg tendé pestle-rhythm song
lineage: Tuareg desert song tradition of the southern Sahara — Niger's Azawagh basin, the Aïr Mountains, southern Algerian Hoggar, northern Mali Adagh-n-Ifoghas, and the Tassili-n-Ajjer plateau. The tendé pestle-drum (wooden mortar with stretched goatskin head, struck in alternation by two women using wooden pestles) anchors the rhythm while two further women hold the mortar steady — the four-woman configuration is canonical. Women sing antiphonal call-and-response over the tendé pulse, with men sometimes responding from a separate position; men of high social rank participate in the parallel takamba ceremonial repertoire on tehardent three-string lute. The repertoire spans courtship songs, camel-praise songs (the canonical Saharan poetic-praise form), and ceremonial cycles tied to the Festival in the Desert traditions that pre-date the modern eponymous festival. Caroline Card-Wendt's 1976-1978 doctoral fieldwork in the Azawagh (Tuareg Music and Social Identity, Indiana 1982), the AIMP/VDE-Gallo Niger series, Smithsonian Folkways FE 4470 (1960), and the Ocora Nomades du Niger catalog constitute the documentary anchors. Distinguished from sub-Saharan West African griot traditions by Tuareg's pestle-drum-with-women-singers (vs kora-or-balafon-with-griot-singer) instrumental configuration; distinguished from Wolof and Mandé Sahel by the Tamasheq Berber language and Saharan-pastoral repertoire base.
